entries.1:1: This book is presented as the words of a teacher, a descendant of David who ruled as king in Jerusalem. It tells the reader to expect the reflections of a wise, experienced royal voice.
entries.1:2: The teacher says everything in life feels pointless and empty, like chasing nothing. It invites the reader to take seriously how fleeting and unsatisfying life can seem.
entries.1:3: He asks what a person really gains from all their hard work on earth. It makes the reader weigh whether their labor produces anything lasting.
entries.1:4: Generations come and go, but the earth keeps standing. It reminds the reader that human lives pass quickly while the world goes on.
entries.1:5: The sun rises, sets, and hurries back to rise again. It pictures life as a constant, repetitive cycle the reader can see every day.
entries.1:6: The wind keeps blowing south and turning north, going around endlessly. It shows the reader the same restless, repeating pattern in nature.
entries.1:7: Rivers keep flowing into the sea, yet the sea never fills up, so the water keeps returning to flow again. It illustrates how effort keeps repeating without reaching a final goal.
entries.1:8: Everything is exhausting, and no one can fully put it into words; our eyes and ears are never satisfied with what they take in. It tells the reader that endless seeking and watching never truly satisfy.
entries.1:9: What has happened before will happen again, and nothing under the sun is genuinely new. It prepares the reader to see life's events as repeating patterns rather than fresh surprises.
entries.1:10: When people call something new, it has actually existed long before us. It warns the reader not to be fooled into thinking their own era is completely different.
entries.1:11: People who lived before are not remembered, and those who come later will not be remembered by those after them either. It reminds the reader that fame and memory fade.
entries.1:12: The teacher identifies himself as having been king over Israel in Jerusalem. It grounds his observations in real authority and personal experience.
entries.1:13: He set his heart on using wisdom to investigate everything done on earth, and he calls this a burdensome task God has given people. It tells the reader that the deep search for meaning is hard work, not easy answers.
entries.1:14: After seeing everything done on earth, he concludes it is all pointless, like trying to catch the wind. It encourages the reader to be honest about how much human effort seems to accomplish.
entries.1:15: What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is missing cannot be counted. It reminds the reader that some problems and gaps in life simply cannot be fixed by us.
entries.1:16: He tells himself he has become greater and wiser than anyone before him in Jerusalem, with much wisdom and knowledge. It shows the reader how far he went in his pursuit of understanding.
entries.1:17: He set out to understand wisdom and also foolishness, and concluded this too was like chasing the wind. It warns the reader that even studying everything closely can leave you empty.
entries.1:18: More wisdom brings more grief, and more knowledge brings more sorrow. It tells the reader that learning more about life can also mean feeling more pain.
entries.2:1: The writer decided to test whether pleasure and fun could make life meaningful, but it left him empty. It means chasing good times alone won't satisfy you.
entries.2:2: He concluded that constant laughter and partying are pointless and don't add real value to life. It warns that fun by itself can't give life meaning.
entries.2:3: He tried wine and pleasure while still trying to stay wise, wanting to find out what is actually good for people to do in their short lives. It shows he experimented honestly to find real answers.
entries.2:4: He threw himself into big building projects, like houses and vineyards, to see if achievement would satisfy him. It means big accomplishments alone don't fill the emptiness.
entries.2:5: He planted elaborate gardens and orchards with every kind of fruit tree. It shows he tried creating beauty and abundance, yet it still wasn't enough.
entries.2:6: He built water pools to irrigate his growing trees. It means he invested heavily in his projects, but effort alone doesn't bring lasting meaning.
entries.2:7: He accumulated servants, livestock, and wealth greater than anyone before him in Jerusalem. It shows that even having everything you could want doesn't guarantee satisfaction.
entries.2:8: He gathered silver, gold, treasures, singers, and many women for pleasure. It means piling up luxuries and pleasures still leaves the heart unsatisfied.
entries.2:9: He became greater than anyone before him and kept his wisdom through it all. It shows success and smarts together still don't answer life's deepest questions.
entries.2:10: He denied himself nothing he wanted and enjoyed his work while doing it. It means enjoying what you do is a real reward, but it's temporary.
entries.2:11: When he looked back at everything he built and did, it all felt meaningless and empty, like chasing the wind. It means achievements alone can't give lasting profit.
entries.2:12: He turned to compare wisdom with foolishness, realizing any future king will just repeat what he did. It means no one finds a completely new answer to life's puzzle.
entries.2:13: He saw that wisdom is clearly better than foolishness, just as light is better than darkness. It means being wise is genuinely valuable, even if it doesn't solve everything.
entries.2:14: A wise person sees where they're going while a fool stumbles in the dark, yet both end up with the same fate. It means wisdom helps, but death comes to everyone equally.
entries.2:15: He realized the same fate awaits him as the fool, so he questioned why he bothered being so wise, and concluded it was pointless. It means wisdom can feel worthless when everyone dies the same.
entries.2:16: Neither the wise nor the fool is remembered forever; both fade from memory and both die. It means being remembered isn't guaranteed, so fame can't be your purpose.
entries.2:17: He came to hate life because everything under the sun seemed empty and like chasing wind. It means life can feel crushing when you focus only on what's temporary.
entries.2:18: He hated all his hard work because he'd have to leave it to whoever came after him. It means working only to accumulate things you can't keep is frustrating.
entries.2:19: He had no idea whether his heir would be wise or foolish, yet that person would control everything he built. It means you can't control what happens to your legacy.
entries.2:20: He sank into grief and despair over all the hard work and wisdom he'd poured out. It means realizing your efforts may be wasted can be deeply painful.
entries.2:21: Someone works skillfully and wisely, then leaves it all to a person who did nothing to earn it. It means life often feels unfair, and that's a real grief.
entries.2:22: He asked what a person actually gains from all their hard work and worry under the sun. It means constant striving leaves you asking what it was all for.
entries.2:23: A person's days are full of sorrow and grief, and even at night their mind won't rest. It means overwork and worry rob you of peace, which is pointless.
entries.2:24: He concluded the best a person can do is eat, drink, and enjoy their work, and that this enjoyment comes from God. It means simple daily pleasures are a gift worth receiving.
entries.2:25: No one can truly enjoy food or pleasure without God being the source of it. It means real enjoyment of life comes from God, not just from things.
entries.2:26: God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to those who please him, while sinners just pile up wealth for others to enjoy. It means God rewards those who follow him, and hoarding wealth is ultimately empty.
entries.3:1: Life has a set timing for everything that happens. You can't force events to fit your schedule, so accept that some things come only when their time arrives.
entries.3:2: Birth and death, planting and pulling up plants, all happen at their appointed moments. Your life will include beginnings and endings you don't control.
entries.3:3: There are times when ending something or healing is right, and times to tear down or build up. Not every action is right in every season, so pay attention to what your situation calls for.
entries.3:4: Grieving and laughing, sadness and dancing each have their proper place. Don't feel guilty for sorrow, and don't be afraid to enjoy joy when it comes.
entries.3:5: Some seasons call for gathering and closeness, others for letting go and keeping distance. Wisdom means knowing which season you are in.
entries.3:6: Sometimes you search and gain, sometimes you lose; sometimes you hold on, sometimes you give away. Holding everything tightly isn't always right.
entries.3:7: There is a time to mend and a time to leave things torn, a time to stay silent and a time to speak. Knowing when to talk and when to be quiet is real wisdom.
entries.3:8: Love and hate, war and peace each have their moments in human life. This doesn't excuse hatred; it observes that life contains both conflict and calm.
entries.3:9: The writer asks what a person actually gains from all their hard work. It's a question worth asking yourself about what your labor really earns you.
entries.3:10: God has given people work to do, and the writer has watched them carry it out. Your daily tasks are part of a burden God has placed on humanity.
entries.3:11: God makes everything fitting in its time, yet he has kept people from fully understanding his plan from beginning to end. You can trust God's timing even when you can't see the whole picture.
entries.3:12: The writer concludes that the best thing for a person is to be happy and do good while alive. Enjoyment and kindness are worthwhile ways to spend your life.
entries.3:13: Eating, drinking, and finding joy in your work is itself a gift from God. Simple pleasures are not trivial; they are gifts to receive with thanks.
entries.3:14: Whatever God does lasts forever and cannot be added to or removed. This should make you stand in awe of God rather than try to improve on his work.
entries.3:15: What exists now has existed before, and what will be already is, because God calls the past to account. History repeats, and God is not done with it.
entries.3:16: The writer saw evil even where justice should be, in courts and places of righteousness. Don't be shocked when wrongdoing appears even in places that should be fair.
entries.3:17: God will judge both good and bad people, because he has set a time for every purpose and deed. Justice may be delayed, but it is not forgotten.
entries.3:18: God allows people to be tested so they can see they are like animals in their mortality. This is a humbling reminder that you are not as self-sufficient as you think.
entries.3:19: People and animals share the same fate: both die and both have the same breath. Human beings are not superior in death, so live humbly.
entries.3:20: Everyone and everything comes from dust and returns to dust. Your body is temporary, which should shape how you value your days.
entries.3:21: No one can be certain whether the human spirit rises to heaven or the animal spirit goes down to earth. This is an honest admission of human limits, not a denial of God.
entries.3:22: The writer concludes that enjoying your work is the best you can do, since it is your reward now. No one can show you what will happen after you, so receive today's good with gratitude.
entries.4:1: The writer looks at the world and sees people being treated cruelly, with no one to comfort them, while those doing wrong hold the power. It reminds the reader that injustice is real and painful, and that having no comforter makes suffering worse.
entries.4:2: Because life holds so much misery, the writer says the dead seem better off than the living. This is the honest cry of someone overwhelmed by suffering, not a command to give up on life.
entries.4:3: He goes further and says the happiest seem to be those never born, since they never saw the evil done in the world. It shows how deeply evil can darken a person's view of life.
entries.4:4: He observes that much hard work and success comes from wanting to outdo a neighbor. That kind of envy-driven effort leaves a person empty, like chasing the wind.
entries.4:5: The foolish person sits idle with folded hands and ends up harming himself. Doing nothing out of laziness is its own kind of self-destruction.
entries.4:6: A little with peace is better than a lot gained through endless struggle and chasing after more. It encourages the reader to value rest over restless striving.
entries.4:7: The writer returns to point out another example of life that seems pointless. He is building toward the picture of a lonely worker in the next verse.
entries.4:8: He describes a man alone with no family who works endlessly and never feels he has enough, asking himself who he is really working for. It warns that wealth without relationships or enjoyment is a bitter, empty pursuit.
entries.4:9: Two people working together get more done and share a better result than one alone. It shows the practical value of partnership.
entries.4:10: If one person falls, the other can help him up, but someone alone has no one to lift him. It reminds the reader that we need others when we stumble.
entries.4:11: Two people lying together keep warm, but one person alone cannot keep warm by himself. It is a simple picture of how companionship meets basic human needs.
entries.4:12: One person alone can be overpowered, but two can defend each other, and a rope of three strands is hard to break. It shows that added support makes a person stronger and safer.
entries.4:13: A poor young person who listens to wisdom is better than an old king who is foolish and refuses advice. It teaches that wisdom and teachability matter more than age or status.
entries.4:14: The poor young man may rise from prison to become king, even though he was born poor in that kingdom. It shows that circumstances can change and humble beginnings do not limit a person.
entries.4:15: The writer sees crowds of living people following the young man who will replace the king. It pictures how people flock to a new leader with hope.
entries.4:16: Even with countless people following him, later generations will not be pleased with him either. It warns that popularity and power are temporary and ultimately unsatisfying.
entries.5:1: Going to worship God is serious, so watch how you come and be ready to listen rather than just going through the motions. God cares more about a listening heart than about empty religious actions.
entries.5:2: Don't rush to speak or make big promises to God, since he is in heaven and you are on earth. Fewer, more careful words are wiser than a flood of talk.
entries.5:3: Just as too much work fills your head with dreams, too much talking reveals a foolish heart. Watch your words, because a lot of talk often means little sense.
entries.5:4: If you promise God you will do something, do it soon and don't delay. God is not pleased with people who make promises and then break them.
entries.5:5: It is better to never make a promise to God than to make one and fail to keep it. Be careful about what you commit to, because keeping your word matters.
entries.5:6: Don't let careless words lead you into sin, and don't try to excuse a broken promise by calling it a mistake. God takes your words seriously and can hold back the good you hoped to do.
entries.5:7: Dreams and endless talk often amount to nothing, so don't build your life on them. Instead, live with a healthy respect for God.
entries.5:8: When you see the poor treated badly and justice twisted in a country, don't be shocked, because officials watch over each other and there are higher powers above them. God sees it all, even when it looks like no one is in charge.
entries.5:9: A country benefits when its land is cared for and worked, and having a ruler helps make that possible. Good order matters for the well-being of ordinary people.
entries.5:10: People who love money never feel they have enough, and those who chase wealth are never satisfied with their profits. Chasing more and more leaves you empty.
entries.5:11: When your goods increase, so do the people who want a share of them, so the owner gains little beyond looking at his stuff. Having more often means more people to please and less real benefit.
entries.5:12: A working person sleeps well whether they have little or much to eat, but a rich person who is full often can't sleep. Simple work and enough food bring more rest than abundance.
entries.5:13: I have seen a serious problem: wealth hoarded by its owner ends up hurting him. What you cling to can become the very thing that ruins you.
entries.5:14: Wealth can be lost through bad luck or disaster, leaving a man with nothing to pass on to his son. Money is uncertain and can vanish no matter how carefully you guard it.
entries.5:15: We come into the world with nothing and leave with nothing, and none of our hard work can be carried out with us. Don't build your life as if your possessions will last forever.
entries.5:16: It is a real tragedy that a person leaves the world exactly as he came, with nothing to show for all his labor. Working only for what you can't keep is like chasing the wind.
entries.5:17: Such a person spends his days in gloom, with much sorrow, pain, sickness, and trouble. A life spent only on wealth can end up full of misery.
entries.5:18: I have seen that it is good and right to eat, drink, and enjoy your work during the days God gives you. That simple enjoyment is your reward, so receive it thankfully.
entries.5:19: When God gives someone money, possessions, and the ability to enjoy them and take pleasure in their work, that is a gift from God. Enjoyment of what you have is itself a blessing from him.
entries.5:20: Such a person doesn't worry much about how short life is, because God fills his heart with joy. Joy from God helps you live without being consumed by the passing of time.
entries.6:1: The writer has seen a real problem in ordinary life that weighs heavily on people. It's worth noticing that life under the sun often brings troubles that hit everyone.
entries.6:2: Someone can be given money, possessions, and respect and still not be able to enjoy any of it, and then a stranger ends up with it all. Having plenty does not guarantee happiness, so don't assume wealth equals a good life.
entries.6:3: Even a man with a huge family and a very long life may get no pleasure from good things and no honor when he dies, so a child who never lived at all is better off than he is. Long life and many children are not what make a life worthwhile.
entries.6:4: A stillborn child comes and goes without meaning, and its name is soon forgotten. Some lives seem to vanish without leaving a trace.
entries.6:5: That child never saw the sun or knew anything, yet it is better off than the man who had everything but no enjoyment. Not having lived can seem better than living without any good in it.
entries.6:6: Even if a person lived two thousand years but never enjoyed anything good, it makes no difference, because everyone ends up in the same place. A long life without enjoyment gains nothing in the end.
entries.6:7: People work hard just to feed themselves, yet they are never fully satisfied. Hard work meets basic needs but does not quiet the deeper hunger inside us.
entries.6:8: The wise person has no real advantage over the fool, and the poor person gains nothing by acting wisely. Wisdom and cleverness do not by themselves make life better.
entries.6:9: It is better to enjoy what you actually have than to keep chasing what you want. Endless wanting is empty and just chasing the wind.
entries.6:10: Whatever exists has already been named and is known, and no one can argue with someone stronger than himself. We are limited and cannot fight against what is beyond our control.
entries.6:11: The more words people pile up, the less it helps, since it all comes to nothing. Talking more does not solve the problem or gain anyone anything.
entries.6:12: No one can say what is truly good for a person during a short life that passes like a shadow, and no one can tell what will happen after them. We cannot know the future, so we should hold our plans humbly.
entries.7:1: A good reputation is worth more than expensive perfume, and the day you die is better than the day you were born. What people remember about your character matters more than wealth or a big start in life.
entries.7:2: It's better to visit a place of mourning than a place of partying, because death is where everyone ends up and it makes the living think about their own lives. Being around grief can teach you something that fun never will.
entries.7:3: Sadness can be better than laughter, because a serious face often means a mind that's learning and growing. Hard times can do more for you than easy ones.
entries.7:4: Wise people are drawn to places of sorrow, while foolish people are drawn to places of fun. What you're attracted to says something about how wise you are.
entries.7:5: It's better to listen to a wise person's criticism than to enjoy a fool's singing. Honest correction helps you more than pleasant nonsense.
entries.7:6: A fool's laughter is like thorns crackling under a pot — loud and quick but gone in a moment, and it accomplishes nothing. Don't be impressed by noise that has no substance.
entries.7:7: Cruelty and bribery can twist even a wise person and ruin their heart. Power and money can corrupt anyone, so be careful.
entries.7:8: Finishing something is better than starting it, and being patient and humble is better than being proud. Stick with things to the end and keep your ego in check.
entries.7:9: Don't be quick to get angry, because anger is what fools hold onto. Slow down before you react.
entries.7:10: Don't keep saying the old days were better than today, because that kind of question doesn't come from wisdom. Looking back with longing won't help you live well now.
entries.7:11: Wisdom, especially when paired with an inheritance, is good and benefits everyone alive. Wisdom plus resources is a real advantage.
entries.7:12: Wisdom protects you the way money does, but wisdom is better because it keeps its owner alive. Both help, but wisdom matters more.
entries.7:13: Think about what God has done — no one can straighten what he has made crooked. Some things in life are beyond your control, so accept them.
entries.7:14: Enjoy good times and think carefully in bad times, since God allows both so you can't predict what's coming. Take each season as it comes.
entries.7:15: I've seen good people die young despite their goodness, and wicked people live long despite their evil. Life doesn't always reward people the way you'd expect.
entries.7:16: Don't try to be excessively righteous or overly wise, or you may destroy yourself. Being obsessive about your own goodness can backfire.
entries.7:17: Don't be excessively wicked or foolish either, or you may die before your time. Avoid both extremes.
entries.7:18: Hold onto one thing without letting go of the other; the person who fears God will avoid both extremes. Balance and reverence for God keep you on track.
entries.7:19: Wisdom makes a wise person stronger than ten rulers in a city. Real wisdom is a powerful thing to have.
entries.7:20: No one on earth is so righteous that they always do good and never sin. Don't expect perfection from yourself or anyone else.
entries.7:21: Don't listen to everything people say, or you might hear your own servant cursing you. Paying attention to every comment will only hurt you.
entries.7:22: You know in your heart that you've cursed others many times yourself. Remember your own faults before judging what others say about you.
entries.7:23: I tested all this with wisdom and decided to be wise, but it was beyond my reach. Some things are simply too deep for us to fully figure out.
entries.7:24: What really is, is far off and very deep — who can understand it? Ultimate understanding is beyond human grasp.
entries.7:25: I set my mind to learn and search out wisdom and the reason for things, and to show that wickedness is foolish and folly is madness. Serious study can reveal what's really behind human behavior.
entries.7:26: I found something more bitter than death: a woman whose heart is traps and nets and whose hands are chains. The one who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is caught. This is the writer's warning about a seductive, dangerous person.
entries.7:27: "Look," says the Teacher, "this is what I found, adding one thing to another to get the true account." He's reporting the results of careful, step-by-step investigation.
entries.7:28: My soul is still searching but hasn't found it: I found one man among a thousand, but not one woman among all of them. This is the writer's personal observation, not a rule about all people.
entries.7:29: This alone I found: God made people upright, but they've gone off searching for all kinds of schemes. We were made good, but we've complicated things with our own inventions.
entries.8:1: Wisdom makes a person stand out and even brightens their face, softening a hard expression. It means the reader should value wisdom because it changes how a person looks and carries themselves.
entries.8:2: Obey the king because you made a promise before God to do so. For the reader, this means keeping your word and respecting authority is a serious matter.
entries.8:3: Don't rush to leave the king's presence or get tangled in a bad plan, since he can do whatever he wants. It warns the reader not to be quick to rebel or scheme against those in power.
entries.8:4: A king's word carries authority, and no one can challenge him by asking what he is doing. The reader should recognize that those in power can act, and questioning them openly is risky.
entries.8:5: Whoever obeys the law avoids trouble, and a wise person knows the right time and way to act. It means the reader should obey rules and use good judgment about timing.
entries.8:6: Every purpose has its proper time and way, though people's troubles weigh heavily on them. The reader should accept that timing matters and that life brings heavy burdens.
entries.8:7: No one knows what will happen next, and no one can tell another person when it will happen. It means the reader should humbly admit they cannot predict the future.
entries.8:8: No one controls the wind or the day they die, and no one is free from danger in war, nor does evil rescue the sinner. The reader should accept that some things are simply beyond human control.
entries.8:9: The writer observed all that happens under the sun, including times when one person has power over another and uses it to hurt them. It means the reader should be aware that people in power can cause harm.
entries.8:10: The writer saw wicked people buried and honored, even those connected to the holy place, and they were praised in the town for what they did. It means the reader should not be surprised when bad people receive honor.
entries.8:11: Because punishment for wrongdoing doesn't come quickly, people's hearts become fully set on doing evil. It warns the reader that delayed consequences can make people bold in doing wrong.
entries.8:12: Even if a sinner does wrong a hundred times and lives long, the writer is sure it will go well for those who fear God. It means the reader can trust that respecting God is ultimately worth it.
entries.8:13: It will not go well for the evildoer; their days will not last long like a passing shadow, because they do not fear God. The reader is reminded that a life without respect for God does not last.
entries.8:14: There is a pointless thing on earth: good people get the same treatment as the wicked, and wicked people get what good people deserve. It means the reader should expect life to sometimes seem unfair.
entries.8:15: The writer praised joy, saying there is nothing better under the sun than to eat, drink, and be happy, because that joy stays with a person through their work all the days God gives them. It means the reader should enjoy simple good things in life as a gift from God.
entries.8:16: The writer applied his mind to know wisdom and to observe the busy work done on earth, including people who never sleep day or night. It means the reader should recognize how much restless effort people pour into their work.
entries.8:17: The writer saw all God's work and concluded that people cannot fully understand what happens under the sun, no matter how hard they search, even if they are wise. It means the reader should humbly accept that some of God's ways are beyond human understanding.
entries.9:1: The writer says that good and wise people are in God's hands, but even they can't tell whether life will bring them good or bad. We should trust God with our future instead of expecting to know how things will turn out.
entries.9:2: Everyone ends up with the same fate, whether they are good or bad, religious or not. This reminds us that death comes to all people, so we shouldn't assume our goodness guarantees an easy life.
entries.9:3: The writer calls it a sad fact that everyone dies the same way, and people's hearts are full of wrong while they live. It's a warning to take our own hearts seriously rather than assuming we have plenty of time.
entries.9:4: As long as someone is alive, there is hope, and even a lowly living dog is better off than a dead lion. Being alive is a gift, so we should value the life we still have.
entries.9:5: The living know they will die, but the dead know nothing and are no longer remembered. This should move us to live thoughtfully now, while we still can.
entries.9:6: Love, hate, and envy all end at death, and the dead no longer share in what happens on earth. Our feelings and actions matter now, because there is no second chance after death.
entries.9:7: The writer tells us to eat our food happily and drink with a glad heart, because God is pleased with what we do. Enjoying simple daily gifts is good and right.
entries.9:8: White clothes and oil for the head were signs of joy and celebration. We should carry a cheerful, grateful attitude through our days.
entries.9:9: Enjoy life with the person you love during the short life God gives you, because that is your share in all your work. Love and simple joy are real gifts worth cherishing.
entries.9:10: Do whatever you do with all your strength, because there is no work or planning in the grave. Put your whole effort into the good you can do now.
entries.9:11: The fastest don't always win and the strongest don't always succeed; wise and skilled people don't always get rich or respected, because time and chance affect everyone. We shouldn't be proud or bitter, since life is unpredictable.
entries.9:12: No one knows when their time will come; people are caught suddenly like fish in a net or birds in a trap. We should live ready, because trouble can arrive without warning.
entries.9:13: The writer says he saw an example of wisdom that impressed him. He is about to tell a story that shows how valuable wisdom really is.
entries.9:14: A small town with few people was attacked by a great king who surrounded it with siege works. It sets up a situation where a weak town faced a powerful threat.
entries.9:15: A poor but wise man in the town saved it by his wisdom, yet nobody remembered him afterward. Good deeds are often forgotten, but they still matter.
entries.9:16: The writer concludes that wisdom is better than strength, even though people often ignore a poor person's wisdom and won't listen to them. We should value wisdom itself, not just the status of the person giving it.
entries.9:17: Quiet words from a wise person are heard better than the loud shouting of a ruler among fools. Calm, wise advice is worth more than noisy foolishness.
entries.9:18: Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner can destroy a lot of good. A single wrong choice can undo much that is good, so we should guard our actions.
entries.10:1: A tiny bit of foolishness can ruin a lot of good, the way a few dead flies spoil a whole jar of perfume. Even a little wisdom is worth more than impressive-looking foolishness, so guard your character in small things.
entries.10:2: A wise person's inner direction leads toward what is right, while a fool's leads toward what is wrong. What you set your heart toward shapes where your life actually goes.
entries.10:3: A fool shows his lack of sense even in ordinary daily life, and everyone can see it. Foolishness is hard to hide, so it's worth building real understanding.
entries.10:4: If a powerful person gets angry at you, don't storm off; stay calm and quiet. Staying composed can defuse a situation and keep small trouble from becoming big.
entries.10:5: The writer points to a real problem he has observed: sometimes those in authority make careless mistakes. Leaders don't always get things right, so don't be shocked when they don't.
entries.10:6: Foolish people sometimes end up in important positions while capable people are pushed down. Life isn't always fair, so don't assume rank always matches ability.
entries.10:7: The writer has seen servants riding high while rulers walk like servants, a picture of things turned upside down. Status can flip unexpectedly, so don't put your trust in position.
entries.10:8: Someone digging a trap for others may fall into it himself, and a person breaking through a wall can get bitten by a snake. Schemes to harm others often backfire on the schemer.
entries.10:9: Quarrying stone or cutting wood can hurt the one doing the work. Even good, ordinary work carries risks, so be careful and don't assume effort is safe.
entries.10:10: A dull axe means much harder work, but sharpening it first makes the job go well. Working smart with wisdom saves effort, not just working harder.
entries.10:11: If a snake bites before it's charmed, the charmer's skill comes too late to help. Timing matters, and wisdom means acting before trouble strikes rather than after.
entries.10:12: A wise person's words win people over, but a fool's own words bring him trouble. What you say has real consequences, so choose your words carefully.
entries.10:13: A fool's talk starts out silly and ends up in serious wrong. Foolish speech tends to get worse the longer it goes on, so know when to stop talking.
entries.10:14: Fools talk on and on, yet no one knows what the future holds or what will happen after them. Since we can't predict the future, humble, careful speech beats endless talk.
entries.10:15: A fool wears himself out with his work because he doesn't even know the way to town. Lack of basic understanding makes life harder than it needs to be.
entries.10:16: A land is in trouble when its leader is immature and its officials party early in the day. Good leadership matters, and self-indulgent leaders harm the people under them.
entries.10:17: A land does well when its ruler is of good character and its officials eat at proper times for strength, not for indulgence. Responsible leadership and self-control bring blessing to everyone.
entries.10:18: If no one fixes the roof, it caves in, and idle hands let water into the house. Neglect and laziness cause real damage, so keep up with the work in front of you.
entries.10:19: Feasting brings laughter and wine cheers people up, but both cost money. Enjoyment is fine, yet it has a price, so be honest about what pleasure costs you.
entries.10:20: Don't curse the king or the rich even in your private thoughts, because word travels in surprising ways. Be careful what you think and say about powerful people, since secrets rarely stay secret.
entries.11:1: Be generous and take risks with what you have, even when you can't see any result. In time, your kindness may come back to you in ways you didn't expect.
entries.11:2: Share what you have with many people, not just one or two, because you don't know what hard times may come. Spreading your help around protects you when trouble arrives.
entries.11:3: Rain falls and trees lie where they fall, whether we like it or not. Some things in life simply happen beyond our control, so we should accept them rather than fight them.
entries.11:4: If you wait for perfect conditions before you act, you'll never get anything done. Watching the weather forever means the seed never gets planted, so do the work even when things aren't ideal.
entries.11:5: You can't explain how wind moves or how a baby grows inside its mother, and you can't explain everything God does either. Accept that some things are beyond your understanding and trust God with them.
entries.11:6: Work hard from morning to evening and keep at it, because you don't know which effort will succeed. Do your part and leave the results to God.
entries.11:7: Sunlight is pleasant and it's good to be alive and see the world. Enjoy the simple good things of life while you have them.
entries.11:8: Even if you live a long, happy life, remember that hard days will come too. Enjoy your years, but stay realistic about the difficulties ahead.
entries.11:9: Young people should enjoy their youth and follow what makes them happy. But remember that God sees everything you do, so enjoy life with that in mind.
entries.11:10: Let go of worry and sadness, because youth passes quickly. Don't waste your best years carrying troubles you don't need to carry.
entries.12:1: Remember God while you are young and strong, before old age comes and life stops feeling enjoyable. Start with God now rather than waiting until your best years are gone.
entries.12:2: This pictures the light of life dimming, like sun, moon, and stars going dark and clouds returning after rain. It means hard times will come, so don't put off what matters.
entries.12:3: The body's strength fades: arms tremble, legs bend, teeth grow few, and eyes grow dim. It's a picture of aging, a reminder that our bodies won't last forever.
entries.12:4: Life grows quiet: the street door stays shut, the sound of grinding fades, the bird's song is faint, and music loses its joy. It means the lively sounds of life will one day grow still.
entries.12:5: Old age brings fear of heights and dangers on the road, while the almond tree blossoms white and even small burdens feel heavy; desire fades and mourning begins. It means death is coming for everyone, so live with that in mind.
entries.12:6: The silver cord, golden bowl, jar, and wheel are pictures of life breaking apart at death. It means life is fragile and will one day end, so don't treat it as endless.
entries.12:7: At death the body returns to the dust of the earth, and the spirit returns to God who gave it. It means your life came from God and will answer to him.
entries.12:8: The Preacher repeats his theme: everything done apart from God feels empty and pointless. It means life without God leaves you with nothing lasting.
entries.12:9: The Preacher was wise and shared what he knew, carefully searching out and arranging many wise sayings. It means wisdom is worth passing on to others.
entries.12:10: He looked for words that were pleasant to hear but also honest and true. It means good teaching should be both kind and accurate.
entries.12:11: Wise words stick and prod like sharp goads and firmly driven nails, and they come from one shepherd. It means good teaching may sting a little but it comes from God and helps you.
entries.12:12: Beyond all this, be warned: writing books never ends, and too much study tires you out. It means don't chase endless learning as if it were the point of life.
entries.12:13: Here is the bottom line: honor God and obey his commands, because this is what every person is meant to do. It means the whole of life comes down to trusting and obeying God.
entries.12:14: God will bring every deed into judgment, including hidden things, whether good or evil. It means nothing is truly secret, so live honestly before God.
